Prepared: 06 September 2026

Scope: concise, citable comparison of sodium‑ion (Na‑ion) and lithium‑ion (Li‑ion) battery technologies with emphasis on residential/home energy storage (typical metrics, safety, supply chain, recycling, representative products, deployments). Each major numeric claim lists at least one source in the bibliography below.

---

## Executive summary (one paragraph)

As of the sources collected here, lithium‑ion (in particular LFP — lithium iron phosphate — for stationary/home use) is the established technology for residential battery systems: widely commercialized, UL‑listed systems, known pack-level round‑trip efficiency ≈90%, mature recycling and installed supply chains, and many residential products (e.g., Tesla Powerwall). Sodium‑ion is an emerging, promising alternative offering lower raw‑material cost (sodium abundant), potentially very long cycle life for some chemistries, and good low‑temperature performance; however, Na‑ion commercialization is currently concentrated in industrial/telecom/utility stationary markets and early manufacturer pilot products (CATL, Natron, others). For most homeowners today the safer, better‑documented choice is lithium‑ion (LFP chemistry specifically); Na‑ion may become attractive for residential systems when residential‑grade system integrators, UL 9540 system listings, and local installer ecosystems are widely available.

---

## Summary table (high‑level)

- Sodium‑ion (Na‑ion): Energy density (cell-level) commonly reported in literature/manufacturer announcements: ~100–175 Wh/kg for current commercial prototypes and first‑gen products; some lab/press claims higher (up to 300 Wh/kg or more). Cycle life claims vary widely by chemistry: several thousand cycles up to manufacturer claims of tens of thousands (company‑specific). Round‑trip efficiency generally reported in the mid‑80s to low‑90s % range depending on system and power electronics. Commercial deployments so far focus on telecom, data‑center backup and utility ESS; residential product offerings are limited as of these sources. Sodium raw material (Na) is abundant; cathode/anode chemistries use less or no cobalt/nickel in some designs (lower critical‑metal exposure). Recycling pathways less mature than Li‑ion at scale.

- Lithium‑ion (Li‑ion) for home batteries (stationary focus, typically LFP or NMC variants adapted for stationary use): cell‑level energy density varies by chemistry — LFP ≈90–160 Wh/kg, NMC ≈150–250 Wh/kg (typical ranges reported in reviews). Pack prices for lithium‑ion fell rapidly: BNEF reported pack averages around $108/kWh (2025 survey) and stationary LFP pack prices even lower in some reports (~$70/kWh); installed residential system costs vary by market but typical US installed residential systems (10–14 kWh lithium‑ion) have mid‑range total installed costs in the low thousands to mid‑$10k range (site‑ and country‑dependent). Cycle life: LFP pack designs routinely claim thousands to many thousands of cycles (3,000–6,000+ depending on DOD and BOS). Round‑trip efficiency for packaged residential systems commonly ≈85–95%; Tesla Powerwall datasheet lists 90% RTE and 13.5 kWh usable energy as an example residential product.

---

## Detailed attributes — Sodium‑ion

- Energy density
  - Reported, commercial/near‑commercial sodium‑ion cells: commonly ~100–175 Wh/kg in multiple manufacturer announcements (CATL 160 Wh/kg, other vendors 170–175 Wh/kg) [CATL; pv‑magazine; Notebookcheck] [see refs 4,7,6]. Some lab or early prototype claims report much higher numbers (claims up to 300–458 Wh/kg in press releases or small‑scale research reports) — treat high numbers as research results not mature commercial pack specs [sodiumbatteryhub; energynews] [refs 1,8].

- Cost per kWh (manufacturing and installed/system)
  - Public reporting on Na‑ion pack manufacturing cost is limited; industry commentary emphasizes lower raw‑material cost because sodium is abundant and cheaper than lithium. CATL and other suppliers position Na‑ion as lower cost per kWh for cells vs certain Li chemistries, but independent, audited pack‑level cost studies for residential Na‑ion are not widely published in the sources collected here [CATL press; industry reporting] [refs 4,11]. Installed residential system pricing for sodium‑ion residential products is not broadly available: most deployments are in industrial/telecom, not mass residential markets (price signals therefore limited) [Natron; energy‑storage.news] [refs 15,16].

- Cycle life (cycles at recommended DOD)
  - Range of claims: several thousand cycles (2,000+ reported by some vendors) up to claims of tens of thousands for specific chemistries. Example: Natron (Prussian‑blue sodium‑ion variant for fast power/backup) advertises very high cycle life (company claims 50,000+ cycles for particular products); other sodium‑ion vendors and pilots report 2,000–10,000 cycles depending on formulation and test conditions [Natron; pknergy; highstar] [refs 15,17,18]. Note: wide variance is manufacturer‑specific and test‑protocol dependent.

- Calendar life (years)
  - Long calendar life is sometimes claimed for select Na‑ion formulations, but public, independent field data is limited as of these sources. Many press/industry pieces emphasize high cycle life rather than long calendar life estimates; expect conservative commercial warranties to lag until more field data exists [industry press] [refs 1,11,15].

- Round‑trip efficiency (%)
  - System RTE depends on cells and power electronics. CATL notes system electronics adaptations for Na‑ion and reports approaches to improve system RTE; typical numbers reported in press/industry commentary place Na‑ion round‑trip efficiency in the mid‑80s to low‑90s %, but validated pack‑level numbers for residential Na‑ion products are sparse in these sources [CATL news] [refs 12,13].

- Typical usable depth of discharge (DoD)
  - No widely published standard DoD for Na‑ion residential packs in the public domain yet; vendors that target stationary backup/power quality often design products for 80% DoD or similar to maximize usable energy, but this is manufacturer and product dependent [Natron product pages and industry articles] [refs 15,16].

- Temperature operating range and thermal management needs
  - Several Na‑ion vendors highlight improved high‑temperature tolerance and competitive low‑temperature performance (some Na‑ion chemistries maintain capacity at low temps). Manufacturer datasheets and press suggest Na‑ion cells can operate across wide temperature ranges, but system thermal management practices vary and residential integrators will still need BMS and enclosure thermal design for long life [CATL; Notebookcheck; Natron] [refs 4,6,15].

- Safety incidents / thermal runaway risk
  - Sodium‑ion proponents emphasize chemistry designs with lower flammability risk vs some high‑energy Li‑ion chemistries (some Na‑ion cathodes/anodes avoid transition metals that increase thermal risk). However, Na‑ion is new in commercial stationary settings and large‑scale independent safety incident datasets are not yet available in the collected sources. Some Na‑ion products have obtained safety standards for UL 1973 (backup) or are being field‑validated, but UL 9540A/system listings for residential ESS are not yet as broadly documented as for incumbent Li‑ion residential systems in these sources [Natron; CATL news] [refs 15,12].

- Material supply chain and scarcity
  - Sodium (Na) is abundant and low‑cost (a major advantage). Na‑ion cells can be designed to avoid or greatly reduce use of critical metals like cobalt and nickel, reducing exposure to supply bottlenecks. However, precursor materials for electrodes and electrolytes still depend on industrial chemical supply chains and processing capacity; large‑scale manufacturing ramp will be required to realize low costs [CATL; industry reporting; Wikipedia sodiu"}
